lessons.title: GO TO
intro: So far the computer read your cards from top to bottom, once. GO TO changes that: GO TO 20 jumps straight to the card with statement number 20 and carries on from there.
Any statement can have a number in columns 1–5, not just FORMATs. The numbers don't have to be in order: they're names, not positions.
Jumping forward skips cards. Jumping backward runs cards again, and that's the start of every loop.

exercises.explanation: The number is a label: the computer looks for the card with 50 in columns 1–5 and continues there.
GO TO 20 jumps over the card I = 99, so I is still 1.

exercises.prompt: Do statement numbers have to be in order, like 10, 20, 30?
options: No, any number from 1 to 99999 in any order
exercises.explanation: Labels are names. Many programmers still used 10, 20, 30 … to leave room for new cards.

exercises.prompt: Skip the card that sets X to zero.
exercises.explanation: Jump to 40, the WRITE. GO TO 50 would jump to a FORMAT, which isn't a statement you can run.

exercises.prompt: This job stops with *ERROR*. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: There is no card with the number 30. GO TO 20 would work.

exercises.prompt: In 1968, Edsger Dijkstra wrote a famous letter: "Go To Statement Considered Harmful". What was his point?
options: Too many jumps make a program hard to follow
GO TO only works on IBM machines
exercises.explanation: Programs full of jumps were called spaghetti code. Later languages replaced most GO TOs with loops and blocks, but in 1957 GO TO was all there was.

lessons.title: The Three-Way IF
intro: The original FORTRAN had exactly one way to decide: IF (expression) n1, n2, n3. It works out the expression and jumps to n1 if it's negative, n2 if it's zero, n3 if it's positive.
It's called the arithmetic IF, and it matched an instruction of the IBM 704, which could test a number for minus, zero or plus in one go.
To compare two values, subtract them: IF (A - B) 10, 20, 30 jumps to 10 when A is smaller, 20 when they're equal, 30 when A is bigger. After each branch, a GO TO keeps the others from running too.

exercises.prompt: K is 0. Where does IF (K) 10, 20, 30 jump?
options: Nowhere, it goes to the next card
exercises.explanation: Negative → first number, zero → second, positive → third.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask "is A bigger than B?" with the three-way IF?
options: IF (A - B) 10, 10, 30, and A is bigger at 30
exercises.explanation: A - B is positive exactly when A is bigger. Both other cases can go to the same label.

exercises.prompt: Jump to 99 when N is negative.
exercises.explanation: The first label is for negative values.
5 - 5 is zero, so the IF jumps to 20.

exercises.prompt: In the example, what would X = -4.0 print if both GO TO 50 cards were missing?
exercises.explanation: After a jump, the computer simply reads on. Without GO TO 50, it falls through into the other branches.

exercises.prompt: Why is it called the arithmetic IF?
options: It decides by the sign of a number
It was invented by a mathematician
It does arithmetic instead of jumping
exercises.explanation: Negative, zero or positive: the decision comes from arithmetic, not from a true/false question.

lessons.title: Loops by Hand
intro: With a counter, a jump back and an IF, you can repeat cards as often as you like. That's how the first FORTRAN programmers wrote loops.
I = I + 1 isn't an equation: it means "take I, add 1, store it back in I". Then IF (I - 3) 10, 10, 30 jumps back to 10 while I is 3 or less, and goes on to 30 once I is bigger.
Forget to count up, and the loop never ends. The operator would see the job run and run, and stop it by hand.

exercises.explanation: = means "store" in FORTRAN. The right side is worked out first, then stored on the left.

exercises.prompt: How many lines does this deck print?
exercises.explanation: I goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. When I becomes 6, I - 5 is positive and the IF jumps to 30.
While I - 10 is negative or zero, it jumps back. At 11 it stops.

exercises.prompt: Stack the cards for a loop that prints 1, 2 and 3.
exercises.explanation: Set the counter, print, count up, then jump back. In a deck with jumps, every card has its place.

exercises.prompt: This job never stops. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: All three labels jump back to 10, so the loop can never leave. The last one has to be 30.

exercises.prompt: Little Carl Friedrich Gauss had to add the numbers from 1 to 100 at school. His answer, and the one a loop gives:
exercises.explanation: Gauss saw 50 pairs that each add up to 101. The computer just adds all hundred numbers, which is easy with a loop.
